claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability during cooling and thermal exposure is governed by competition between chemical ordering and sluggish diffusion.
Al has a strong chemical affinity for Ni and Fe in this alloy.
The chemical affinity of Al for Ni and Fe drives formation of ordered intermetallic phases.
Diffusion in high-entropy alloys is characteristically sluggish.
Sluggish diffusion delays phase-transformation kinetics in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Delayed transformation kinetics can allow disordered BCC to persist during cooling.
The balance between the thermodynamic driving force for ordering and kinetic barriers determines the resulting phase stability.
Faster cooling suppresses formation of ordered intermetallic phases.
Faster cooling favors retention of disordered BCC.
Slower cooling promotes formation of ordered B2 or L21 phases.
Prolonged isothermal annealing at intermediate temperatures promotes formation of ordered B2 or L21 phases.
Rapid quenching from the high-temperature BCC state is expected to retain a predominantly disordered BCC structure.
The mechanism should apply over cooling-rate and annealing-temperature ranges where Al and transition-metal diffusion is slow enough to control transformation.
The mechanism may also apply to compositionally similar, Al-containing high-entropy alloys having high-temperature BCC structures.
The mechanism may not apply to alloys with significantly different compositions or crystal structures.
The mechanism may not apply at extremely high cooling rates such as quenching.
The mechanism may not apply at very high annealing temperatures where diffusion is extremely rapid.
The cooling rates and annealing temperatures needed to produce the proposed ordering transition are not established.

contradictions.description: Faster cooling and rapid quenching are used to predict and define retention of disordered BCC, but the boundary simultaneously says that the hypothesis may not apply at extremely high cooling rates such as quenching.
Formation of ordered phases at high cooling rates is declared falsifying, although the stated boundary potentially excludes high-rate quenching from the hypothesis's domain.
